**Conversation Overview**

The person shared a Markdown report analyzing Edexcel A-Level Further Mathematics Core Pure (9FM0) past papers and asked Claude to convert it into an interactive, accessible HTML file. The report contained detailed data on 83 knowledge points across CP1 and CP2 papers spanning 2019–2025, including topic frequency, mark allocations, difficulty ratings, priority classifications, hidden recurring techniques, and revision recommendations.

Claude read the uploaded report file and a frontend design skill document, then planned and built a comprehensive single-page HTML dashboard saved to the outputs directory. The finished file features a dark academic visual theme with a sticky tabbed navigation bar organizing six sections: Overview (with stat cards, top-10 topic table, rare high-mark topic table, and never-tested alerts), Priority Matrix (fully searchable and filterable table of all 83 topics with sort-by-column functionality and priority/chapter chip filters), Hidden Techniques (accordion-style expandable cards), Difficulty Analysis (animated bar chart plus hardest and easiest topic tables), CP1 vs CP2 Comparison (side-by-side leaning tables and exclusive-topic table), and Recommendations (interactive checklist with session-state checkboxes). All topic data was encoded directly in JavaScript within the HTML file, making it fully self-contained and openable in any browser without a server.

The domain terminology used throughout includes spec references (e.g., "9FM0," "CP1/CP2"), mathematical topic names (De Moivre's theorem, SHM, integrating factor, Maclaurin series, coupled DEs), priority bands (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/REVIEW/NEVER), and difficulty ratings (Easy/Medium/Hard/Very Hard). The person made no corrections or follow-up requests during the conversation.

The person shared an HTML dashboard they had built after auditing past papers for the Edexcel A-Level Further Mathematics specification, specifically the Core Pure component. They asked Claude to redesign the dashboard to look nicer and more approachable while preserving all existing data. The dashboard contained detailed topic-level audit information including frequency analysis, priority matrices, difficulty ratings, hidden traps, a chapter explorer with collapsible accordions, an interactive question finder with JavaScript filtering, and a low-confidence topics table.

Claude began by thoroughly reading the original 5,946-line HTML file across multiple passes to understand its complete structure and content across all eleven sections: Start Here overview cards, Priority Matrix, Urgent Topics, Frequent High-Mark topics, Easy Marks revision cards, Hardest Topics table, Hidden Traps, Chapter Explorer, Question Finder, and Low Confidence table. ### 1. Overview
This report is based on the JSON audit files in `/tmp/core_pure_audit/`. It is written for revision planning, not for predicting an exam paper with certainty.

#### Last Week Before Exams
- Prioritise high-mark recurring skills: differential-equation modelling and evaluation, SHM/damped motion, polar area, De Moivre, matrix inverses, vectors with planes, volumes of revolution, and Maclaurin series.
- Do mixed questions rather than isolated textbook drills. The data shows many hard questions are hard because they combine a main method with a secondary skill.
- Build a checklist for hidden moves: conjugate roots, partial fractions before integration, inverse hyperbolic log form, determinant non-zero condition, exact domain restrictions, and long-term model checks.
- Be aware of 2 specification topics that have **never appeared** in any past paper: 3D transformations (3x3 matrices) and Euler exponential form. These could appear as a surprise, especially if the examiners want to test breadth.
- For each practice question, write one sentence after marking it: “What was the hidden step?” This is faster than redoing whole papers and targets the mistakes that cost method marks.

#### With More Time
- Work chapter by chapter first, then switch to paper-mixed practice. Start with the high-priority matrix, then cover the review band so no specification area is completely unfamiliar.
- For rare high-mark topics, do one full worked example and one unassisted example. Matrix modelling, forced vibration, related rates, and parametric/volume questions deserve this treatment.
- Keep an error log split into algebra slips, setup errors, interpretation errors, and exact-form errors. Those categories match the patterns seen in hard questions.
- Revisit accessible frequent topics such as basic De Moivre, matrix determinants, and hyperbolic identities for quick marks, but do not spend all revision time there.

#### How to Use the Dashboard File
Use `/tmp/core_pure_audit/core_pure_topic_audit_dashboard.html` as a targeting tool. Filter by chapter when you want focused revision, sort by marks when choosing high-impact topics, and use the frequency bands to decide whether a topic needs full practice or a short review. A sensible workflow is:

1. Sort by total marks and pick one high-priority topic.
2. Open the listed example papers and attempt the relevant question parts under timed conditions.
3. Check the mark scheme for the hidden technique, not just the final answer.
4. Add the topic to either “secure”, “needs another question”, or “needs notes first”.

Final caution: this report shows what has happened in the analysed papers, not what must happen next. The best revision plan uses the data to avoid blind spots while still building broad Core Pure fluency.

**Conversation Overview**

The person shared an HTML dashboard they had built after auditing past papers for the Edexcel A-Level Further Mathematics specification, specifically the Core Pure component. They asked Claude to redesign the dashboard to look nicer and more approachable while preserving all existing data. The dashboard contained detailed topic-level audit information including frequency analysis, priority matrices, difficulty ratings, hidden traps, a chapter explorer with collapsible accordions, an interactive question finder with JavaScript filtering, and a low-confidence topics table.

Claude began by thoroughly reading the original 5,946-line HTML file across multiple passes to understand its complete structure and content across all eleven sections: Start Here overview cards, Priority Matrix, Urgent Topics, Frequent High-Mark topics, Easy Marks revision cards, Hardest Topics table, Hidden Traps, Chapter Explorer, Question Finder, and Low Confidence table.
